question: Explain how natural selection can change a population over generations.
student_answer: A population begins with inherited variation, so individuals do not all have the same traits. In a particular environment, some inherited traits make survival or reproduction more likely. Individuals with those traits tend to leave more offspring, and those offspring can inherit the helpful traits. Across many generations, the helpful traits become more common in the population. Individuals do not choose to evolve, and a single organism does not change its genes because it needs to. The population changes because variants have different reproductive success. For example, suppose a beetle population contains inherited green and brown color variants. If birds more easily see green beetles on dark soil, brown beetles may survive and reproduce at a higher rate. Their offspring are more likely to inherit brown coloration. After many generations, brown coloration may be much more common, although mutation and migration can continue to add variation. The environment matters because the same trait might not be helpful on pale sand. Natural selection therefore depends on heritable variation, environmental pressure, differential reproductive success, and time. This answer also notes that chance can affect small populations, but genetic drift is a different mechanism from natural selection. Repeating the central point: inherited differences influence which organisms leave offspring, and allele frequencies in the population can consequently change over generations. The result is adaptation at the population level, not a purposeful change by an individual organism.

criteria.name: Mechanism
criteria.description: Connects heritable variation, environmental pressure, and differential reproduction.

criteria.name: Population change
criteria.description: Explains change over generations without implying individual choice.

teacher_feedback: Accurate, but far beyond the requested length.
